title: Roy Palmer, Fess and Bill's lessons
summary: Palmer's style, and Bill's own first lessons and teaching Eddie Pearson.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Learning your horn: teachers, lessons and fees

blocks.x: How was Roy Palmer? What style did he have?

Palmer? Uh huh. Palmer was in between them. Roy Palmer. He was a good musician. Baratone and trombone. He played at the villa. One place, one spot all the time. Him and the old dude you see the old piano around you, play around you, all that you see. And he was playing there with Fess. Old Fess had charge of the band. I don't know if he told you about it. He mentioned it once.
Did you ever play with Fess at all? That's right. Have you played with Fess?

I played with Fess. My first lesson I took when I was learning how to read, I went to Fess and lived on Ellick Street in Algeria. He told me to get a little Tesson's Catechism. I said, boy you done improved mighty quick on that horn. Woo woo. I said, well begin from that catechism you start from. That's all. Like the people talk about Eddie Pearson. Steve Lewis was learning how to play trombone. And Steve Lewis didn't make you, bought a brand new horn. And Eddie Pearson come to my heart and say, that was, that was when I first married this guy, I said, I will learn how to play trombone like you. Eddie always was a man, you understand? He was in my class, you see Eddie. I was about seven, eight years old then but I mean we all come up together. See? I said, okay I'll learn you what I know. You know we're all together. I said, I learned Eddie was driving a truck right there for the cigar factory. I said, I'll learn you what I know. Like that. So he come back to my house over there in Algeria's. Started taking, well take lessons. He had a boss Steve Lewis home. I said, why don't you go to Vic? He taught me. So now I'm right over here with you. You can show me what you got but you know, I know the other fellas ain't going to do it. They won't take time out and ask them. I said, how about Fess? He said, Fess will show you. Fess didn't charge him too much money. He wants something for nothing. I said, I've been a young man, you know. So I said, okay. I said, first man, line eight is where the B flat was on the horn and everything. He took last one he bought, say about a year and eight months. Well, we had to go over the lake, you know. So we had to go over the lake every summer and I come back and be waiting. When I come in, he start telling what to do, the books and everything. And so next time he went to Fess. So Fess said, man, that boy sure doesn't improve on that horn. You sure? He said, you told him. I said, well. I told him all I know Fess. That's all I could do. He said, yeah, he doesn't improve. I can't do nothing with him. So Ada was gone. He told lots of people, many people that I taught him. It's like little Bob Aran right now. He learned him how to play. He learned him how to read drum music. George Williams. Nice. We learned him. Happy. We learned him. Had to learn Happy because we had the big band. They had Cecil Thornton, a great arranger from St. Louis. You don't know him. He had come down and he joined the Celestate band and he was the one that put Ricard to back. Trent Celestate band. He started arrangements there. He ceased the thorn. He was good on it. He was working on the cap. He got him a wife from now and he stayed down there and he started arranging for Papa Celestate. That's why he had put so much stuff on Ricard on the shoppers. I tell him that all the time. Even in fact, St. Louis, he's still in the mail service now. I can think so much about this life.
